title: the WSG mountaineering proficiency
audit_comment: The mountaineering slice pins the essential tools and skills (pitons - metal spikes pounded into cracks for a line anchor, never handholds or footholds; the special hammer, a weapon hammer will not do; the placement knowledge only a mountaineer has), the mountaineer-led roped ascent (one mountaineer enables the whole group on a surface they could not climb, if all are roped together and he leads), the piton-as-anchor uses (a belayer backup, a rappel anchor, a chasm-crossing tie point), and the piton loosen rules (a 10% come-loose chance, checked the first time it supports 100 pounds or more; a passed check stays lodged until a mountaineer dislodges it; a 10% chance a secured piton cannot be dislodged and must be left behind) (rules/wsgmntnr.h, prefix wmt); census 370 -> 371.

banner.title: The WSG THE MOUNTAINEERING PROFICIENCY, R446: the mountaineer prose (no table this round) - a proficient character is only slightly more accomplished than any other non-thief on most non-horizontal surfaces where his special equipment offers no advantage, but when a difficult surface must be ascended or descended his presence can mean the difference between life and death. The essential tools and skills: PITONS, specially crafted metal spikes pounded into small cracks and fissures in a rock face to provide an anchor for a line - they are NOT used as handholds or footholds (uncomfortable at best, dangerous at worst, the surface area of a secured piton is not very large); a SPECIAL HAMMER to pound them in (a weapon hammer is the wrong material and too unwieldy to swing perched on a cliff); and the KNOWLEDGE of where to place them so they hold and give the greatest support - anyone can drive a piton into a crack, but only a mountaineer can tell which cracks will not widen or crumble. One mountaineer enables everyone else in the group to ascend or descend a surface they could not climb without him, as long as all the characters are roped together and the mountaineer is in the lead. Pitons also serve as a backup for a belayer, an anchor for someone rappelling, and a place to tie a rope before crossing a chasm. No matter the use or the strain, a piton has only a 10% chance of coming loose, checked the FIRST time it supports 100 pounds or more (simply pulling the rope does not count); a piton that passes stays lodged until a mountaineer dislodges it with his hammer - and there is a 10% chance any secured piton cannot be dislodged and must be left behind. Census 370 -> 371.

banner.sentinel: A piton has a 10% chance of coming loose, checked the first time it supports 100 pounds or more; a passed check stays lodged until a mountaineer dislodges it - and a secured piton has a 10% chance of refusing to come out at all and being left behind.

consts.name: wmtLoosenPct
consts.comment: No matter what a piton is used for or how much strain is put on it, there is only a 10% chance that it will come loose.

consts.name: wmtFirstCheckLbs
consts.comment: The loosen chance is checked the first time the piton is called upon to support a weight of 100 pounds or more; simply pulling on the rope will not dislodge a piton or indicate whether it has a chance of coming loose.

consts.name: wmtStuckPct
consts.comment: There is a 10% chance that any secured piton will not be able to be dislodged and must be left behind.

bools.name: wmtSlightlyBetterWithoutGear
bools.comment: A character with proficiency in mountaineering is only slightly more accomplished than any other non-thief at climbing or traversing most non-horizontal surfaces where his special equipment is not needed or offers no advantage.

bools.name: wmtLifeAndDeathOnDifficult
bools.comment: When a difficult surface must be ascended or descended by members of an adventuring party, the presence of a mountaineer can mean the difference between life and death.

bools.name: wmtPitonsAreAnchorsNotHolds
bools.comment: Pitons are specially crafted metal spikes pounded into small cracks and fissures in a rock face to provide an anchor for a line - contrary to popular conception, they are NOT used as handholds or footholds: uncomfortable at best, dangerous at worst, since the surface area of a secured piton is not very large.

bools.name: wmtSpecialHammerRequired
bools.comment: A special hammer is used to pound the pitons into the rock face; a hammer that serves as a weapon will not do - wrong material, and far too unwieldy to swing while perched on the side of a cliff.

bools.name: wmtPlacementKnowledge
bools.comment: The third essential skill is the knowledge of where to place the pitons so they hold and give the greatest support - anyone, conceivably, can drive a piton into a crack, but only a mountaineer can tell which cracks will not widen or crumble so the piton has only a small chance of coming loose.

bools.name: wmtLeadsRopedGroup
bools.comment: One mountaineer in a group can enable everyone else to ascend or descend a surface they could not climb without him, as long as all the characters are roped together and the mountaineer is in the lead.

bools.name: wmtPitonBackupForBelayer
bools.comment: A piton will serve as a backup for a belayer, provide an anchor for someone rappelling, or serve as a place to tie a rope before crossing a chasm.

bools.name: wmtPassedCheckStaysLodged
bools.comment: If the piton passes the first loosen check, it will remain lodged until a mountaineer dislodges it with his hammer.

bools.name: wmtStuckMustBeLeftBehind
bools.comment: There is a 10% chance that any secured piton will not be able to be dislodged and must be left behind.

examples.note: the two piton chances: a 10% come-loose chance on the first load, and a 10% cannot-be-dislodged chance on removal
the first-check threshold: the loosen chance is checked the first time the piton supports 100 pounds or more
the piton arithmetic anchor: the two chances are equal at 10, and the 100-pound threshold is ten times the loosen percentage

table_checks.note: all three piton numbers are positive: a real chance, a real chance, a real threshold
the printed pair: the 10% chance at the 100-pound check - both digits exactly as the book prints them
